Leo Strauss — (1899–1973), political philosopher. On his relationship with Schmitt, see Heinrich Meier, Carl Schmitt, Leo Strauss und „Der Begriff des Politischen“. Zu einem Dialog unter Abwesenden, 3rd ed., Stuttgart/Weimar 2013.

Walter Benjamin — (1892–1940), philosopher, literary critic, and translator. See Susanne Heil, „Gefährliche Beziehung“. Walter Benjamin und Carl Schmitt, Stuttgart/Weimar 1996; Michael Rumpf (ed.), “Briefwechsel Michael Rumpf – Carl Schmitt.” In: Schmittiana NF II, 2014, pp. 275–285.

under the impact of the words “sacrifice for life …” — Schmitt repeatedly worked through Benjamin’s book on German tragic drama with great intensity; see Reinhard Mehring, “Geist ist das Vermögen, Diktatur auszuüben. Carl Schmitts Marginalien zu Walter Benjamin.” In: idem, Kriegstechniker des Begriffs. Biographische Studien zu Carl Schmitt, Tübingen 2014, pp. 132–152; Jürgen Thaler, “Genial. Carl Schmitt liest Walter Benjamin.” In: Marcel Atze/Volker Kaukoreit (eds.), Lesespuren – Spurenlesen oder Wie kommt die Handschrift ins Buch? Von sprechenden und stummen Annotationen, Vienna 2011, pp. 246–251.
Pleasure conceives and gives birth to sin — 1 John 2:16; see above, p. 315.
Michel Mourre, Lamennais p. 141 — Michel Mourre, Lamennais ou l’hérésie des temps modernes, Paris 1955.
Have I not done exactly the same myself with Adam Müller — In: PR.

The world in which Prof. Wilhelm Grewe’s little light shines — Grewe, who from 1950 onward advised Adenauer in negotiations with the victorious powers of the Second World War, took part in the 1955 trip to Moscow. There he was less willing than Adenauer to make concessions to the Soviets. He is regarded as the originator of the Hallstein Doctrine.

The full-blooded Moju can do that better — This refers to Moritz Julius Bonn, who took part in the negotiations over the Treaty of Versailles as a member of the German delegation in 1919 and was appointed adviser to the Reich Chancellor on reparations in 1920.

Johann Jacob Reiske — (1716–1774), German scholar of Greek, Arabic, and Byzantine studies. In his works, Wilamowitz-Moellendorff repeatedly drew attention to Reiske’s philological achievements, which went unrecognized for many years.
Come along, Cohn — From Theodor Fontane’s poem “An meinem Fünfundsiebzigsten” (“On My Seventy-Fifth Birthday”), which ends:
I was something to everyone, They all read me, They had all known me for ages, And that is the main thing … “come along, Cohn.”

the anti-Roman feeling of the historian Fritz Kern — Kern (1884–1950) became Schmitt’s colleague at the University of Bonn in 1922. On 5 May 1923 Schmitt wrote about him in his diary: “I dislike him; a Protestant professor.” (Tb 1921–24, p. 192). Kern converted to Catholicism in 1949.
“That is the true taking of land” —

“Again and again, from the tangled outlines of the Littorale, the Saracen tower emerged, gradually growing smaller as the perspective changed, a pale shape amid the solitude of rock and sea. At every bend I was glad to see it again, the guardian of a southern territory that had become for me a piece of spiritual homeland. That is the true taking of land.”
E. Jünger, Sämtliche Werke, vol. 6, p. 315.

Konrad Beyerle — (1872–1933), jurist and politician, co-author of the Weimar Constitution. Article 153 of the Weimar Constitution—corresponding to Article 14 of the German Basic Law—guaranteed property, but also stated:
“Property entails obligations. Its use should also serve the common good.”

This led to a debate lasting several years over the expropriation of the former princely houses. A popular initiative supported expropriation in 1926, but the referendum that followed did not. The attempted expropriation of the princes therefore failed.

My cousin André — André Steinlein (1891–1964), son of the younger brother of Schmitt’s mother, whom Schmitt had known since their school days. On 16 December 1954, Schmitt wrote to Nicolaus Sombart about his ambivalent relationship with him:

“…But I still have to coordinate matters with my Lorraine cousin, an aging bon vivant who, after a typically bourgeois life as a notary, has retreated into a rural backwater on the Seille. Yet, from old habit—we have somehow kept running into one another ever since our youth—I am very fond of him; if only because the old saying applies to him in a typical way: il n’y a pas de notaire qui n’ait rêvé de sultan—there is no notary who has not dreamed of being a sultan.”

Hear the Nobel Prize prophet — This refers to Max Born (1882–1970), who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1954. Schmitt is quoting M. Born, “Das entscheidende Motiv. Eine Erwiderung.” In: Merkur, 1955, no. 92, p. 999.
Alfons Adams — (1899–1973), philosopher, brother of Paul Adams.
Good Friday of the spirit — See G. F. W. Hegel, Glauben und Wissen. In: idem, Werke, ed. Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 2, p. 432. Hegel’s spelling of Karfreitag has been modernized here.
Mount of Olives of world history — See Konrad Weiß, Zum geschichtlichen Gethsemane, Mainz 1919, reprint Bigge n.d. [1945], pp. 185 ff.
Vigens disciplina, Fides moribunda — “The discipline [of the Church] flourishing, faith dying.” Vigens ecclesiae disciplina is a term from canon law.

Wilhelm Wackernagel says — W. Wackernagel (1806–1869), Germanist and art historian, professor in Basel from 1835. Schmitt is referring to Wilhelm Wackernagel, Über die dramatische Poesie, Basel 1838. See Carl Schmitt, Hamlet oder Hekuba, 2nd ed., Stuttgart 1993, p. 51, with note 21 on pp. 72 f. (first published 1956).

report on Adolf Grabowsky — A. Grabowsky (1880–1969), geopolitician, lecturer at the Deutsche Hochschule für Politik from 1921 to 1933, published Gott und der Zauberer. Ein Mythos, Berlin 1912. Schmitt’s report on it is in his papers, RW 265 no. 19394.

Pierre Leyris — (1907–2001), translator and literary critic. Schmitt means: H. Melville, Benito Cereno (Biblioteca Zig Zag, 19), Santiago de Chile 1944. On pp. 130–142 appears P. Leyris, “Reflexiones sobre ‘Benito Cereno’.” Leyris had already published an annotated French translation of Benito Cereno, with a preface, in 1937.
May 1953 in Herrenalb — See the note above on p. 304.
It took that article in the Linksrheinischer Merkur — Eduard Rosenbaum, “Carl Schmitt vor den Toren.” In: Rheinischer Merkur no. 48, 25 November 1950.
Again and again I fell for the deception — Schmitt is quoting himself here: ECS, p. 88; see also the entries above for 11 February 1948 and 11 August 1950.
Friedrich Glum — F. Glum, Philosophen im Spiegel und Zerrspiegel. Deutschlands Weg in den Nationalismus und Nationalsozialismus, Munich 1954.

Rüdiger Altmann — (1922–2000), jurist, political writer, and political adviser. At the end of the war he studied under Schmitt, later under Wolfgang Abendroth. Schmitt quotes the essay “Was heißt christliche Demokratie?” by Friedrich Grund, probably a pseudonym for Rüdiger Altmann. In: Civis. Zeitschrift für christlich-demokratische Politik 2, 1955, no. 11, pp. 57–58. The sentence:
“In fact, today there is no substantive ethic in the Western cultural sphere other than the Christian one”
Karl Korn — K. Korn, “Kyklos. Zu F. G. Jüngers neuen Gedichten.” In: Berliner Hefte für geistiges Leben 3, 1948, pp. 42–55.

La nullité protège mieux. L’ambiguité protège mieux — “Nothingness protects better. Ambiguity protects better.” A variation on Rivarol’s frequently quoted maxim, L’obscurité protège mieux—“Obscurity protects better.” See the note above on p. 158.
With The Origin of Species in 1859 — Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favored Races in the Struggle for Life, London 1859.

“…those who affirm the truth and certainty of the reality of sensory objects [can] be told that they must be sent back to the lowest school of wisdom, namely the ancient Eleusinian mysteries of Ceres and Bacchus, and must first learn the secret of eating bread and drinking wine…”
G. W. F. Hegel, Werke. Edited by Moldenhauer and Michel, vol. 3, Frankfurt am Main 1970, p. 91.
Brothers of the gently living flesh — Thomas Müntzer called Luther “the soft-living flesh of Wittenberg.”
It is the hump … — See above, p. 131.
And powers of delusion … — Theodor Däubler, “Hymne an Sizilien.” In: idem, Dichtungen und Schriften. Edited by Friedhelm Kemp, Munich 1956, p. 86.

Peter Schneider — (1920–2002), Swiss jurist, assistant to Carlo Schmid. In 1955 he completed his postdoctoral qualification with the study Ausnahmezustand und Norm. Eine Studie zur Rechtslehre von Carl Schmitt, Stuttgart 1957. Schmitt first learned of Schneider in 1953 through A. Mohler; see BW Mohler (index) and BW Huber, pp. 374 ff.
Simone Weil, Karl Epting — See the note above on p. 299.
The poor celibate bureaucracy — Schmitt coined the term “celibate bureaucracy” in 1923; see RK, p. 6; Gespräch, p. 57.

Edith Stein, who had herself baptized and became impenetrable within the religious order — E. Stein (1891–1942), philosopher and women’s rights advocate. She converted from Judaism to Catholicism in 1922 and entered the strict Carmelite order. She was murdered at Auschwitz and canonized in 1998.
concept of the chosen one — See the note above on p. 208.
Caux — Swiss resort town, known from 1946 onward as an international conference center for Moral Re-Armament.
Above my cap … — Parody of Goethe; see the note above on p. 170.
Rolf Schroers — (1919–1981), writer; see van Laak, pp. 251–255.

article by Baron von der Heydte in Hochland — Friedrich August von der Heydte, “Heil aus der Gefangenschaft? Carl Schmitt und die Lage der europäischen Rechtswissenschaft.” In: Hochland 43, 1950/51, pp. 288–294; see also the note above on p. 210.

Julian Huxley — (1887–1975), English biologist and researcher of animal behavior. Schmitt is referring to J. Huxley, Entfaltung des Lebens (Fischer Bücherei, 61), Frankfurt am Main/Hamburg 1954. A copy containing annotations is in Schmitt’s papers, RW 265 no. 26715.

all the Walter Ottos and all the Schadewaldts — Walter F. Otto (1874–1958), classical scholar; Wolfgang Schadewaldt (1900–1974), classical scholar. Both studied the continuing influence of Greek mythology and religion.
in an article in Junge Wirtschaft — Winfried Martini, “Ein gefährliches Provisorium.” In: Junge Wirtschaft. Zeitschrift für fortschrittliches Unternehmertum, 1955, no. 11, pp. 404–405.

a poisonous Morgenthau type — This refers to Franz Borkenau (1900–1957), Marxist sociologist and philosopher of history. Schmitt is referring to F. Borkenau, “Spengler – Weitergedacht. Eine Antwort an seine Kritiker.” In: Der Monat 8, 1955, pp. 46–55. The quotation beginning “The malice …” appears on p. 48.
… non canalisata, non canalisabilis — “…not channeled, not capable of being channeled”; see the note above on p. 305.
miching mallecho. It means mischief — See the note above on p. 271.
We Christian folk now have joy — Opening line of a Christmas hymn by Kaspar Füger (1521–1592), also used as an organ chorale by J. S. Bach.
to Sombart, to Jünger — Schmitt’s letter of 26 December 1955 to Nicolaus Sombart ends with the sentence:
“I wish you and your wife happiness and good health in the New Year and remain, on this side and beyond every boundary of age and market, your eternally unchannelable Moselle man.”
(BW Sombart, p. 85). Similar wording in BW EJ, p. 289.

lecture by Hermann Heimpel — The historian Heimpel (1901–1988), professor at the Reich University of Strasbourg from 1941 to 1944 and a friend of E. R. Huber, spoke on NDR—not NWDR—at 6:25 p.m. on 1 January 1956 under the title “Was verlangt das neue Jahr?” (“What Does the New Year Demand?”).

No longer the Jews … — The 1906 Catechism of the Catholic Church stated that Jesus was condemned to death because Pilate “cowardly gave in to the threatening pressure of the people of Jerusalem.” In the 1955 catechism the wording became:
“The Son of God was rejected by the leaders of the chosen people.”
(Kath. Katechismus der Bistümer Deutschlands, Freiburg 1955, p. 53). In the revised catechism of 2005, this became “some leaders.”

Sovereign is he who decides on the state of exception. — Schmitt formulated this not in 1921 but in 1922, in Political Theology. The problem of the exception had, however, already been discussed systematically in 1921 in Carl Schmitt, Die Diktatur. Von den Anfängen des modernen Souveränitätsgedankens bis zum proletarischen Klassenkampf, 6th ed., Berlin 1994, pp. XVII f. and passim.
Exceptions do not count — Not a literal quotation; see Hans Freyer, Theorie des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters, Stuttgart 1955, pp. 157 ff.
about the conversation with Hans Freyer after Wiesbaden — On 6 January 1956, a colloquium on Hans Freyer’s Theorie des gegenwärtigen Zeitalters was held in Wiesbaden.

“The formal feature [of a justification of dictatorship] lies in the authorization by a supreme authority that is legally capable of suspending the law and authorizing a dictatorship—that is, permitting a concrete exception whose content, compared with the other case of a concrete exception, the granting of a pardon, is enormous. Abstractly speaking, the problem of dictatorship would be the problem of the concrete exception, a problem that has so far received little systematic treatment in general legal theory.”
